# jj store

This reference describes the application command parser. See [capabilities](../reference/capabilities.md) for profile and qualification limits.

Manage native JJ repositories over authenticated RPC.

Use `jj store init` for a new repository, or `jj store attach` to create a
physical workspace for an existing repository. Ordinary JJ commands then read
and publish the same native history. Connection metadata contains no
credentials. Use `jj store login` or inject `JJ_STORE_TOKEN`.

Use `jj store migrate-local` inside an existing authenticated workspace to
hydrate a LocalTrusted replica and switch the workspace only after local closure
verification.

Use `jj store help -k commands` for the command guide. Server creation and
administration are separate from physical workspace attachment.


```text
Usage: jj store [OPTIONS] [COMMAND]
```

| Argument or option | Meaning | Default / values |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--format <FORMAT>` | Output presentation. JSON retains full identities, versions and response variants for automation. Inherited by subcommands. | Default: text; Values: text, json |
| `-R, --repository <REPOSITORY>` | Path to repository to operate on  By default, Jujutsu searches for the closest .jj/ directory in an ancestor of the current working directory. Inherited by subcommands. |  |
| `--ignore-working-copy <IGNORE_WORKING_COPY>` | Don't snapshot the working copy, and don't update it  By default, Jujutsu snapshots the working copy at the beginning of every command. The working copy is also updated at the end of the command, if the command modified the working-copy commit (`@`). If you want to avoid snapshotting the working copy and instead see a possibly stale working-copy commit, you can use `--ignore-working-copy`. This may be useful e.g. in a command prompt, especially if you have another process that commits the working copy.  Loading the repository at a specific operation with `--at-operation` implies `--ignore-working-copy`. Inherited by subcommands. | Default: false; Values: true, false |
| `--no-integrate-operation <NO_INTEGRATE_OPERATION>` | Run the command as usual but don't integrate any operations  When this option is given, the operations will still be created as usual but they will not be integrated to the operation log. The working copy will also not be updated.  The command will print the resulting operation ID. You can pass that to e.g. `jj --at-op` to inspect the resulting repo state, or you can pass it to `jj op restore` to restore the repo to that state. You can also pass the ID to `jj op integrate` to integrate the operation.  Note that this does *not* prevent side effects outside the repo. For example, `jj git push --no-integrate-operation` will still perform the push. Inherited by subcommands. | Default: false; Values: true, false |
| `--ignore-immutable <IGNORE_IMMUTABLE>` | Allow rewriting immutable commits  By default, Jujutsu prevents rewriting commits in the configured set of immutable commits. This option disables that check and lets you rewrite any commit but the root commit.  This option only affects the check. It does not affect the `immutable_heads()` revset or the `immutable` template keyword. Inherited by subcommands. | Default: false; Values: true, false |
| `--at-operation, --at-op <AT_OPERATION>` | Operation to load the repo at  Operation to load the repo at. By default, Jujutsu loads the repo at the most recent operation, or at the merge of the divergent operations if any.  You can use `--at-op=<operation ID>` to see what the repo looked like at an earlier operation. For example `jj --at-op=<operation ID> st` will show you what `jj st` would have shown you when the given operation had just finished. `--at-op=@` is pretty much the same as the default except that divergent operations will never be merged.  Use `jj op log` to find the operation ID you want. Any unambiguous prefix of the operation ID is enough.  When loading the repo at an earlier operation, the working copy will be ignored, as if `--ignore-working-copy` had been specified.  It is possible to run mutating commands when loading the repo at an earlier operation. Doing that is equivalent to having run concurrent commands starting at the earlier operation. There's rarely a reason to do that, but it is possible. Inherited by subcommands. |  |

| `--color <WHEN>` | When to colorize output Inherited by subcommands. | Values: always, never, debug, auto |
| `--quiet <QUIET>` | Silence non-primary command output  For example, `jj file list` will still list files, but it won't tell you if the working copy was snapshotted or if descendants were rebased.  Warnings and errors will still be printed. Inherited by subcommands. | Default: false; Values: true, false |

## jj store token

Administer repository-scoped tokens through the authenticated native API.

```sh
jj-store token generate
jj store token list --endpoint https://store.example --repo-id REPOSITORY_ID
jj-store token list --endpoint https://store.example --repo-id REPOSITORY_ID
```

Both command families use the same repository admin credential from the OS
facility or `JJ_STORE_TOKEN`. An operator credential grants no repository
access. Connection flags belong to `list`, `grant`, `revoke`, `status`, and
`retry`; `--format json` returns structured results without a pager.

`generate` creates one manual bearer credential locally, prints it once and does
not store it. Grant that same credential independently to each repository that
it should discover. Repository policies retain separate permissions, expiry and
revocation, so removing it from one repository does not affect the others.

`grant --principal ID --permission read|write|admin --request PATH` adds a
client-generated token. Supply its complete bearer credential through a hidden
prompt, `--token-stdin`, or `JJ_STORE_GRANT_TOKEN`. The grant credential is
separate from the admin credential. Optional `--expires-at UNIX_SECONDS` sets
its expiry. No secret is accepted in arguments, printed, or saved in the
journal.

`revoke --token-id ID --request PATH` removes a grant. Both mutations retain the
exact snapshot, principal, request ID and intent in a bounded local request file
outside checkouts before publication. Existing request files must match the
original intent; a stale request never silently refreshes its snapshot.

`status --request PATH` checks the durable receipt without publishing. An
`unknown` result means no receipt was observed; it does not prove rejection.
`retry --request PATH` reapplies the exact saved request. Grant status/retry
needs the original grant credential through the same hidden/stdin/environment
input; revoke requires none. Keep that credential in its OS facility or secret
manager. Current admin authorization and the original principal are required for
every receipt read. Rotation to another admin token for the same principal is
allowed.

Keep request records for recovery. If a request is stale, inspect current token
state before deliberately creating a new request file. Never overwrite or delete
a journal to make an uncertain publication look like a new operation.



needs the original grant credential through the same hidden/stdin/environment
input; revoke requires none. Keep that credential in its OS facility or secret
manager. Current admin authorization and the original principal are required for
every receipt read. Rotation to another admin token for the same principal is

state before deliberately creating a new request file. Never overwrite or delete

For example `jj --at-op=<operation ID> st` will show you what `jj st` would have shown you when the given operation had just finished. `--at-op=@` is pretty much the same as the default except that divergent operations will never be merged.  Use `jj op log` to find the operation ID you want. Any unambiguous prefix of the operation ID is enough.  When loading the repo at an earlier operation, the working copy will be ignored, as if `--ignore-working-copy` had been specified.  It is possible to run mutating commands when loading the repo at an earlier operation. Doing that is equivalent to having run concurrent commands starting at the earlier operation. There's rarely a reason to do that, but it is possible. Inherited by subcommands. |  |

## jj store token retry

Administer repository-scoped tokens through the authenticated native API.

```sh
jj-store token generate
jj store token list --endpoint https://store.example --repo-id REPOSITORY_ID
jj-store token list --endpoint https://store.example --repo-id REPOSITORY_ID
```

Both command families use the same repository admin credential from the OS
facility or `JJ_STORE_TOKEN`. An operator credential grants no repository
access. Connection flags belong to `list`, `grant`, `revoke`, `status`, and
`retry`; `--format json` returns structured results without a pager.

`generate` creates one manual bearer credential locally, prints it once and does
not store it. Grant that same credential independently to each repository that
it should discover. Repository policies retain separate permissions, expiry and
revocation, so removing it from one repository does not affect the others.

`grant --principal ID --permission read|write|admin --request PATH` adds a
client-generated token. Supply its complete bearer credential through a hidden
prompt, `--token-stdin`, or `JJ_STORE_GRANT_TOKEN`. The grant credential is
separate from the admin credential. Optional `--expires-at UNIX_SECONDS` sets
its expiry. No secret is accepted in arguments, printed, or saved in the
journal.

`revoke --token-id ID --request PATH` removes a grant. Both mutations retain the
exact snapshot, principal, request ID and intent in a bounded local request file
outside checkouts before publication. Existing request files must match the
original intent; a stale request never silently refreshes its snapshot.

`status --request PATH` checks the durable receipt without publishing. An
`unknown` result means no receipt was observed; it does not prove rejection.
`retry --request PATH` reapplies the exact saved request. Grant status/retry
needs the original grant credential through the same hidden/stdin/environment
input; revoke requires none. Keep that credential in its OS facility or secret
manager. Current admin authorization and the original principal are required for
every receipt read. Rotation to another admin token for the same principal is
allowed.

Keep request records for recovery. If a request is stale, inspect current token
state before deliberately creating a new request file. Never overwrite or delete
a journal to make an uncertain publication look like a new operation.

```text
Usage: jj store token retry [OPTIONS] --repo-id <REPO_ID> --request <REQUEST>
```

## jj store init

Create a new native repository and attach its first physical workspace.

```sh
jj store init ./work --endpoint https://store.example
```

The destination must be empty for the first attempt. `--workspace`, `--cache`,
`--state-dir`, `--ca-certificate` and `--insecure-loopback` follow attachment
conventions. Use `jj store attach` for a repository that already exists.

Repository creation requires a separate operator credential, provisioned with
`jj-store operator init` or injected through `JJ_STORE_OPERATOR_TOKEN`. The
initial repository admin credential comes from `JJ_STORE_TOKEN` for automation
or is generated and saved to the OS credential facility before creation. Secrets
are never printed or stored in the checkout or journal.

Retry the same command after an interruption. Its durable local record retains
the repository ID, epoch and credential identity before contacting the server;
attachment resumes with its original operation. Changed options or credentials
fail explicitly. A retry of an acknowledged repository requires current access
but does not need the creation operator. Keep the state directory for recovery.

## jj store serve-local

### Serve a local native repository service

`jj store serve-local --server-config PATH` starts the same foreground service
as `jj-store run` and requires a literal loopback listener. Storage, resource
limits and shutdown behavior come from the generated local configuration.

Create that configuration with `jj-store init --local --state-dir PATH`; it
starts the pinned embedded RustFS helper and reuses its explicit volume on
restart. No daemon, Docker service or repository credential is required.
`config example` documents deferred shared-deployment fields and is not the
local setup path.

On Unix the command hands off to the paired `jj-store` executable in the same
build directory, preserving foreground process ownership and graceful shutdown.
Other platforms should run `jj-store run --loopback-only` directly until their
handoff behavior is qualified.

## jj store attach

Attach a new physical workspace to an existing native repository.

```sh
jj store attach ./work --endpoint https://store.example --repo-id REPOSITORY_ID
```

The destination must be empty. A unique logical workspace name is generated
unless `--workspace` is supplied. Local JJ indexes and store bindings go in a
separate client data directory; `--cache` selects an explicit empty directory
outside the checkout. The workspace initially has an empty working change based
on the root. Use ordinary `jj edit` or `jj new` to select existing history.

Credentials come from `JJ_STORE_TOKEN` or the OS credential facility. TLS
verifies the server hostname and trust chain. `--ca-certificate` adds a
deployment CA. Plain HTTP requires both a literal loopback address and
`--insecure-loopback`. The command never converts a Git repository or prints a
token.

Attachment is resumable. Retry the same command after an uncertain outcome; the
journal retains the operation identity and never stores bearer secrets.
`--state-dir PATH` selects a durable directory outside the checkout. By default
it lives beside an explicit cache under `.jj-store-attachments`, or in the OS
client data directory. Keep that journal until attachment finishes.

A retry must use the same connection, credential, workspace and paths. Repeating
a completed attachment verifies access and returns its original result without
snapshotting files or publishing another operation. Lost or edited journals are
not inferred from workspace names. Do not delete a journal to bypass a pending
operation or name conflict.

```text
Usage: jj store attach [OPTIONS] --repo-id <REPO_ID> <DESTINATION>
```

## jj store migrate-local

### `jj store migrate-local`

Hydrate the current authenticated native workspace into a complete LocalTrusted
repository and atomically switch the workspace to that local server.

```text
jj store migrate-local --unix-socket /absolute/path/native.sock \
  [--cache /absolute/path/local-cache] \
  [--state-dir /absolute/path/migration-state]
```

The source repository must already have replication identity and the local
server must permit LocalTrusted repository creation or already contain the same
logical repository. The command pulls a complete seed and a pinned feed tail,
verifies the working-copy operation from local storage, then switches only
`.jj/repo`. It does not snapshot, update, reconcile, or rewrite working files.

The exact prior `.jj/repo` descriptor is retained as
`.jj/repo.jj-store-remote-v1`. Retries must use the same socket, cache, and
state directory. Credentials remain in the configured OS credential facility or
process environment and are never written to the migration journal.


```text
Usage: jj store migrate-local [OPTIONS] --unix-socket <UNIX_SOCKET>
```

| Argument or option | Meaning | Default / values |
| --- | --- | --- |

## jj store status

Inspect the current native repository heads without changing the checkout.

`jj store status --format json` reports the repository, endpoint, native
profile, and full operation head IDs. Multiple heads remain explicit. This
command never snapshots physical edits or reconciles operations. Use ordinary
`jj log` and `jj op log` for native history; JJ may snapshot when those commands
normally do.

## jj store doctor

Check the local native binding, credentials and remote repository access.

The diagnostic checks bounded metadata, the pinned native profile and current
repository authentication. It reports operation heads without publishing or
changing working-copy state. A failure exits nonzero with a Hint. Use
`--format json` for structured success output.

## jj store capabilities

Report repository capabilities and their current verification scope.

Inside a Git-backed JJ repository, status, doctor and capabilities return the
version-2 local profile. Projects, tasks and comments run directly against the
companion metadata store without a native connection or server. Reading does not
initialize repository metadata or a local actor. Agent and review support is
reported separately as it is qualified. The native version-1 matrix remains
available in native repositories and outside a repository.

`jj store capabilities --format json` returns a versioned command matrix. Native
commit, operation and evolution histories are separate. Git transport commands
require a Git backend and are unsupported on native repositories. Destructive GC
remains disabled. A library test is not executable parity evidence: commands
without direct acceptance are reported as unqualified.

The executable matrix is qualified against jj-cli/jj-lib 0.45.1 on the current
Unix host. Semantic comparisons use an isolated upstream Git-backed reference;
native repositories contain no Git storage. Native IDs have their separate codec
conformance tests. Comparisons omit reference-only `@git` tracking refs.

| Commands or behavior                                      | Acceptance                                                                                        |
| --------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| edit, describe, new, log, diff, op log, evolog            | Executable lifecycle and restart fixtures                                                         |
| bookmark create/set/delete/list                           | Executable lifecycle, including conflicted bookmark reconciliation                                |
| rebase, squash, split, abandon, undo                      | Parent relationships, local bookmarks, descendant content and evolution compared with upstream    |
| multi-parent new; resolve --list; manual conflict editing | Three-sided conflicts and snapshot-based resolution compared with upstream                        |
| file show/list/chmod                                      | Binary bytes, symlink targets, executable modes and copied/renamed file snapshots                 |
| sign and unsign                                           | SSH Ed25519 signing, re-signing, verification and unsigned rewrites; requires a configured signer |
| concurrent operations                                     | Divergent descriptions and conflicted bookmarks reconcile without losing either accepted sibling  |
| Git transport and util gc                                 | Explicit rejection with unchanged publication snapshot                                            |

The named `native_cli_semantic_*` fixtures are in
`crates/jj-store-cli/tests/executable_native.rs`. They use memory-backed RPC and
are distinct from the retained RustFS cold-deployment reports. Filesystem copies
are content/snapshot evidence; complete native copy histories and submodules
have separate codec/backend fixtures because upstream exposes no file-copy
command in this release. External merge tools and other signing backends are not
covered by this matrix. Non-Unix platform qualification remains a release gate;
the ledger records completion.

The standalone TLS/RustFS recovery fixture uses a generated localhost
certificate with explicit client trust and no plaintext override. This qualifies
the production TLS transport on the current host; other deployment topologies
and release platforms remain separate gates.

```text
Usage: jj store capabilities [OPTIONS]
```

## jj store login

Manage repository credentials outside the checkout.

```sh
jj store login --endpoint https://store.example --repo-id REPOSITORY_ID
jj store logout --endpoint https://store.example --repo-id REPOSITORY_ID
```

Login prompts without echo; `--token-stdin` reads one token from stdin for
provisioning. Login verifies access before saving to the OS credential facility.
Credential accounts bind the canonical server URL and repository ID. No
plaintext fallback is provided. Logout removes only that exact account. An
injected `JJ_STORE_TOKEN` overrides the OS facility; logout reports that the
environment must be cleared separately. Never pass a token on the command line.

```text
Usage: jj store login [OPTIONS] --repo-id <REPO_ID>
```

## jj store version

version, source revision, build target and build profile. Use `--format json`
for structured output. Ordinary `jj version` retains upstream behavior.
